intro.data: Currying says a function of a pair, h : C×A → B, is the SAME as a function returning a function, ĥ : C → (A → B), where ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a). On the left are four two-at-once functions; on the right are their curried transposes — plus two impostors. One impostor curries the OTHER argument first; the other is an unrelated map. Match each function to its true transpose and leave the traps unpaired.
intro.alchemy: Staging says a process on two reagents at once, h : C×A → B, is the SAME as one taking the first and yielding a process for the second, ĥ : C → (A → B), where ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a). Left: four two-at-once processes. Right: their staged forms, plus two impostors — one stages the WRONG reagent first, one is unrelated. Match each to its true partner.
intro.spellcraft: Staging says a working on two essences at once, h : C×A → B, is the SAME as one taking the first and yielding a working for the second, ĥ : C → (A → B), where ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a). Left: four two-at-once workings. Right: their staged forms, plus two impostors — one stages the WRONG essence first, one is unrelated. Match each to its true partner.
intro.abstract: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A gives a natural bijection Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A) sending h to its transpose ĥ with ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a). Match each h : C×A → B with its ĥ : C → B^A. Two distractors are offered: one transposes the swapped argument, one is not a transpose at all.

goal.data: Match each of the four two-at-once functions with its correct curried form; reject both impostors.
goal.alchemy: Match each of the four two-at-once processes with its correct staged form; reject both impostors.
goal.spellcraft: Match each of the four two-at-once workings with its correct staged form; reject both impostors.
goal.abstract: Pair each h : C×A → B with the unique ĥ : C → B^A satisfying ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a).

context.data: This is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A — currying. The transpose ĥ must satisfy ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a) for ALL c and a; mishandling either argument breaks the match.
context.alchemy: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: the staged form must satisfy ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a) for every c and a.
context.spellcraft: The adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: the staged form must satisfy ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a) for every c and a.
context.abstract: (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A : Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A), with ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a).

sub.abstract: ĝ(y)(x) = h(x, y), not h(y, x)

sub.abstract: q(x)(y) = x · y ≠ any h(c, a)

afterSuccess.data: All four functions matched exactly one curried form, and BOTH impostors were left unpaired — that one-to-one correspondence IS the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A. The first impostor curried the second argument first, so it computed x − y from (y, x) order: ĝ(y)(x) = h(x, y), not h(y, x) — a different function. The second impostor multiplied instead of subtracting, so it was nobody's transpose. The true transpose must agree with h on EVERY input: ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a).
afterSuccess.alchemy: All four processes matched exactly one staged form, and both impostors stayed unpaired — that correspondence is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, A→B). One impostor staged the wrong reagent first; the other was an unrelated process.
afterSuccess.spellcraft: All four workings matched exactly one staged form, and both impostors stayed unpaired — that correspondence is the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A: Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, A→B). One impostor staged the wrong essence first; the other was an unrelated working.
afterSuccess.abstract: The bijection Hom(C×A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A) sends h to the unique ĥ with ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a); it is natural in C and B, which is exactly the adjunction (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A. The swap impostor is the transpose of h∘swap, a genuinely different arrow; the multiply impostor lies outside the image of any h here. Order matters for non-commutative h, which is why subtraction and exponentiation expose the trap.

reveal.summary: An adjunction F ⊣ G is a natural one-to-one correspondence Hom(F A, B) ≅ Hom(A, G B). Currying is the example (−)×A ⊣ (−)^A, with ĥ(c)(a) = h(c, a). The transpose must agree with h on every input, so currying the wrong argument — or an unrelated map — is not a transpose.
reveal.programmerAnalogy: curry: ((c, a) => b) ↔ (c => a => b). For sub, curry((x,y)=>x-y) is x=>y=>x-y; x=>y=>y-x is curry of the swapped function — a different map.
